summary: 41a covers: the anonymous Sifra follows R. Yehuda (setam Sifra = R. Yehuda); Rav Chisda's ruling that kinnim (bird-pair offerings) are only designated at the moment of slaughter (first slaughtered = chatat); R. Yochanan's counter that explicit prior designation is also binding; multiple kinnim scenarios about what happens when birds die or are mixed up.

learning.ahaMoment: When the Gemara says 'the Sifra' without naming an author, it always means R. Yehuda.
learning.memoryAnchor: Setam Sifra = R. Yehuda - the quiet author behind the Torat Kohanim.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does it matter that an unattributed ruling in the Sifra is assumed to follow R. Yehuda?
learning.coreTension: A ruling stated without a named author could in principle follow any tanna's position, leaving its halachic weight and scope ambiguous until the author is identified.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara states the general attribution rule directly, then applies it to the goat-to-Azazel provisions, fixing their authorship and thereby their legal context.

takeaway.text: When the Sifra states a ruling anonymously, the Gemara treats it as following R. Yehuda's position, a default attribution rule applied here to the goat-to-Azazel provisions.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume anonymous rulings are authorless or universally agreed-upon, missing that the Gemara assigns them a specific, identifiable author by a fixed convention.

display.title: Kinnim: Designated by Slaughter, Not by Intent

learning.ahaMoment: Bird pair designation is activated by the act of slaughter, not by prior intent - the event determines identity.
learning.memoryAnchor: Kinnim identity = determined at slaughter: which is cut first = that becomes the chatat; the survivor becomes the olah.
learning.learnerQuestion: When does a pair of birds (kinnim) become specifically designated as the chatat and the olah?
learning.coreTension: A woman bringing kinnim might intend from the outset which bird is which, yet Rav Chisda holds that intent alone does not fix their identity, raising the question of what actually does.
learning.coreMove: Rav Chisda rules that designation occurs only at the moment of slaughter, the first bird slaughtered for chatat becomes the chatat, while R. Yochanan counters that explicit prior naming is also binding even before slaughter, and the Gemara traces the practical fallout (replacement pairs, mixed-up scenarios) from each position.

takeaway.text: Rav Chisda rules that kinnim are designated only at the moment of slaughter, the first bird slaughtered becomes the chatat and the second the olah; R. Yochanan holds that explicit prior designation is also binding, which determines what happens if a bird dies or the pair gets mixed up before slaughter.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume verbal designation always fixes an offering's identity, missing Rav Chisda's distinct claim that for kinnim specifically, the act of slaughter, not stated intent, is what fixes it.

misconceptions.misconception: A pair of kinnim birds becomes specifically designated the moment the woman says 'this one is the chatat.'
misconceptions.correction: According to Rav Chisda, that statement alone does not fix the designation; the birds remain potentially either the chatat or the olah until the moment of slaughter, when the first one slaughtered becomes the chatat. R. Yochanan disagrees and holds explicit prior naming is binding even before slaughter, the two positions disagree precisely on whether the woman's statement is enough.

rashiTranslations.en: An unattributed Sifra - it is Torat Kohanim, following Rabbi Yehuda; so it says in Sanhedrin
(86a). And this is indeed in Torat Kohanim, since the verse is written in the book of Leviticus:
The bird pairs are not designated - which is for the olah and which is for the chatat - except by the taking of
the owner, etc. If, when he acquired them, he said: this one I take for the olah, and this one for the chatat,
the priest can no longer change them at their performance.
And if he changed them, it is invalid. And if, when he acquired them, he did not
specify, even though he called them by name
afterward, the name does not take effect upon them,
and the priest can change them. 'And she shall take' 'and he shall make' -
regarding the woman after childbirth it is written: and she shall take two turtledoves or
two young pigeons, one for the olah and one
for the chatat; and likewise regarding the metzora, and concerning the zav, the priest shall make
one a chatat and one an olah - proving that
either at the time of taking they are designated, or at the time of
their performance, but in between, no. 'But here' -
etc. From the fact that it is taught here that the lot sanctified,
is it not logical that the name should sanctify? And one might have thought
that the sanctification of the name at the time of the sanctification of the lot
is what is meant, that it is neither the time of taking nor
the time of performance - this is our reading: 'but here' -
that it is neither the time of taking nor the time of performance
it is, yet it is taught that it became fixed. 'One who defiles the Sanctuary' -
one who enters the Sanctuary impure, and he is liable for an offering
that rises and falls with wealth and poverty, and the lowest
tier of poverty stated regarding the oath of utterance
and the oath of testimony; and there too it is written
(Lev. 5): 'or a soul who touches,' etc.,
and we established it in Shevuot (7a)
as referring to impurity of the Sanctuary and its sacred things - that after
he became impure he entered the Sanctuary, or ate
sacred things. 'And he became rich' - and he must bring
according to the wealthy tier. 'And afterward' - he divides the money
and specifies, and says: these are for his chatat, and these
for his olah - even though there is no poor person's offering now
obligating him, but only a rich person's offering, and there is not
in a rich person's offering an olah, only a chatat
of an animal - when he comes before the court, the court will say to him:
'bring a rich person's offering.' 'He adds' - from his own house
up to the price of an animal, and brings his obligation, an animal
from the proceeds which he called by the name chatat. 'And he does not'
add and bring - an animal chatat from the proceeds of
his olah, since he cannot change them into monies
that he set aside, which he called by the name olah, to acquire
from them a chatat. 'But here' - that after
he set them aside he specified, and this is neither taking nor performing - yet it is taught that it became fixed.
The name took effect upon them, and he may not change them. 'And do you think so?' Is this a resolution? But did not
Rabbi Elazar say etc.? And since a poor person's offering is not fit for him even post-facto, how could
the name of olah take effect upon them once he became rich? Behold, he is not obligated for an olah. 'Rather, what'
can you say? Perforce it must be understood as a disruption, and one must say that this word 'and afterward'
that is taught is an error; rather it should properly be taught: 'and he said, these for the chatat,
these for the olah, and afterward he became rich' - since at the time he fixed them an offering was fit for him, and since
perforce it is acknowledged as an emendation, Rav Chisda too resolved it thus: he already said
from the time of separation, and here it is taught: one who defiles the Sanctuary, a poor person, who set aside money for his kinnim-offering

and said at the time of separation: these for the chatat, these for the olah, and afterward became rich - he adds and brings, since separation by money is like the time of taking the birds. 'And according to Rabbi Chagga' - who said

one who defiles the Sanctuary, rich, and brought a poor person's offering, fulfilled his obligation - and because of this it is not disrupted, and this is a resolution, since this offering was fit for him post-facto, he can teach that it became fixed.
